title: Cellar and Portrait
premise: Property surveyor Bram Hartwell arrives at his late grandmother's house to appraise it for sale, armed with skepticism and a checklist. But the house keeps adding things: an extra chair in every old photograph, a thirteenth step on the cellar stairs, and a portrait of a founder whose eyes follow the surveyor's pencil. Bram learns the house was built by four founders who bound a hungry presence beneath the cellar with a harvest-moon ritual, and his grandmother died before her turn in the cycle. As the moon waxes, the house begins appraising Bram in return—measuring his memories, his loyalties, and what he is willing to trade for the truth. In the end, Bram must choose between destroying the inheritance and completing the ritual himself, and he chooses completion, sealing the cellar at the cost of his own portrait joining the wall.
about_author: Isandro Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former land surveyor from the chalk hills of southern England who spent fifteen years cataloguing houses that no one wanted to buy twice. He now writes full-time in a converted tithe barn, where he insists the drafts get colder after midnight.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Bram Hartwell, third-person limited, arrives at his grandmother's house to appraise it for the estate sale. He measures rooms, notes dry rot, and refuses to acknowledge the cold spot in the hallway. Emotional beat: controlled professional detachment beginning to fray at the edges.

chapters.title: Thirteen Steps
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Surveying the cellar, he counts fourteen steps down and thirteen up. He recounts three times, blames fatigue, and chalks the discrepancy on his clipboard. That night, in a motel, he dreams of a chair. Emotional beat: the first crack in his rational armor.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Keep
chapters.summary: Sorting his grandmother's albums, Bram notices an extra wooden chair in every photo spanning sixty years—same chair, same position, even in pictures taken in other houses. Third person. Emotional beat: dread arriving quietly, like an item on an invoice.

chapters.title: The Portrait of Elias Vane
chapters.summary: In the parlor hangs a portrait of founder Elias Vane, dated 1897. When Bram looks away and back, the painted eyes have shifted. He covers the portrait with a drop cloth; the cloth is folded neatly on the floor by morning. Emotional beat: being watched by something patient.

chapters.title: The Founders' Deed
chapters.summary: Bram researches the property at the county records office and finds the original deed lists four founders—Vane, the Ashcombes, and a name scraped away. A clerk mentions the house has never sold; it only ever 'changes hands.' Emotional beat: the past is a contract still being enforced.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic, Bram finds his grandmother's ledger: dates, moon phases, and entries in her handwriting that she could not have written—entries dated after her death. The last line reads, 'Bram is next. Forgive me.' POV Bram. Emotional beat: grief curdling into betrayal.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Elderly neighbor Ruth Ashcombe, descendant of a founder, warns Bram over tea: the house appraises people, and her family's line was 'written off' generations ago. She gives him a tarnished founder's ring. Emotional beat: the relief and terror of being believed.

chapters.title: The Chair Sits Down
chapters.summary: Bram returns to photograph the cellar for his report. In the developed images, the extra chair now sits at the top of the stairs—inside the house, facing his grandmother's bedroom. Third person. Emotional beat: the observation has become occupation.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Missing
chapters.summary: Bram's own belongings begin vanishing and reappearing in the house: his father's watch on the kitchen table, his childhood drawing pinned to the pantry door. The house is cataloguing him. Emotional beat: the hunter's tools turned against the hunter.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door Won't Stay Shut
chapters.summary: Bram nails the cellar door closed; by dawn the nails are on the hallway floor, arranged in a neat row. From below, faintly, the sound of a chair being pulled out. POV Bram. Emotional beat: the invitation he cannot refuse.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth reveals the ritual: every generation, one heir must 'sign the ledger' under the harvest moon to renew the binding, or what the founders buried wakes and collects the town's memories like rent. Her line defaulted in 1961; her mother forgot her own children. Emotional beat: loyalty to family versus truth about what family built.

chapters.title: What the House Appraises
chapters.summary: Bram dreams he stands in a vast cellar office while a faceless clerk reads aloud his life—every lie, every kindness, every debt—stamping pages PASSES or FAILS. He wakes with ink on his palm. Third person. Emotional beat: being measured and found wanting.

chapters.title: The Scraped Name
chapters.summary: Bram matches the scraped name on the deed to a fifth founder: Hartwell. His own ancestor didn't sign the ritual—he was the collateral, bound into the house. The chair in the photographs has always been his family's seat. Emotional beat: inheritance as a trap he was born into.

chapters.title: The Portrait Changes Hands
chapters.summary: Elias Vane's portrait now shows Bram's face, aged fifty years, wearing Vane's coat. Bram burns the portrait; the ashes arrange themselves into a signature. POV Bram. Emotional beat: horror becoming personal, the house claiming authorship of him.

chapters.title: Running Appraisal
chapters.summary: Bram flees to a hotel two counties away. The room's single photograph on the wall gains a chair by morning. He drives back at dusk, understanding there is no outside. Third person. Emotional beat: the collapse of escape as a strategy.

chapters.title: The Founders' Minutes
chapters.summary: In the cellar's hidden alcove, Bram finds the founders' minutes: the thing below is not a demon but the town's unpaid past—every broken promise, every stolen acre—given appetite. The ritual doesn't imprison it; it reconciles the accounts. Emotional beat: the monster is the ledger.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: The moon swells orange over the fields. The house's doors all open inward. Bram, ring on finger, ledger in hand, descends the thirteen steps—now fourteen going down. Ruth stands at the threshold, unable to follow. Emotional beat: resolve forged from having no other door.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Accounts
chapters.summary: Below, the clerk-thing presents Bram's ledger of a life: his failures, his grandmother's sacrifice, his ancestor's theft. It offers a trade—walk away, forget, and live. Bram, POV, must answer. Emotional beat: the temptation of comfortable forgetting.

chapters.title: Signature in Ash
chapters.summary: Climax. Bram refuses to forget and instead reads the accounts aloud himself—naming the founders' crimes, his grandmother's payment, his own—balancing the ledger with truth instead of sacrifice. The house shudders; the chair empties. Emotional beat: loyalty fulfilled through honesty, not obedience.

chapters.title: The New Portrait
chapters.summary: Dawn. The cellar is quiet, the extra chair gone from every photograph—except one new portrait above the parlor fireplace: Bram, painted in the founders' style, eyes forward, at peace. Ruth finds the ledger closed. Emotional beat: victory with a cost written into the frame.

chapters.title: Appraised Fair
chapters.summary: Bram completes his survey, marking the house 'not for sale—held in trust.' The cold spot is gone; the steps count thirteen both ways. He stays as caretaker, writing the next entry in the ledger in his own hand. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed as duty.

chapters.title: Cellar and Portrait
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Bram's POV. Years later, a young woman arrives asking to appraise the house; Bram pours her tea and watches the portrait watch her back. The final image: the painted Bram smiling, just slightly, for the first time. Emotional beat: the cycle continues, but on new terms.
